https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This spreadsheet is the completed Bid Point Calculator and Evaluation Criteria Matrix used by the Troy School District selection committee to score its 2024 food-service management company (FSMC) bids. Three companies were scored: SFE (Southwest Food Service Excellence), ARAMARK, and CHARTWELLS. The matrix allocates up to 100 total points, split between a price component worth 51 points and non-price criteria worth the remaining 49.

The price calculation takes each bidder's price per meal/meal equivalent from lowest to highest, subtracts the lowest bid, divides by the lowest bid, subtracts that ratio from 1, and multiplies by 51. The entered bid prices are $2.906263 for SFE (the lowest), $3.40028016 for Aramark, and $3.43 for Chartwells. This produces price points of 51.00 for SFE, 42.33 for Aramark, and 41.81 for Chartwells -- so the two higher-priced bidders lose only a few points relative to the lowest.

The non-price criteria and their maximum points are: Management Candidate (9 pts, split 7 pts for K-12 breakfast/lunch staffing experience and 2 pts for menu development and special events); Marketing & Merchandising Plan (4); Nutrition Education (2); Past Performance (4); Plan of Operation (4); Plan to Increase Participation (4); District Specific Requirements (8); District Manager Support (2); Employee Training & Development (6); Evaluation of FSMC References (3); Integrity & Reliability of Projected Operating Budget/Forecast (3); and FSMC Guarantees (0). The matrix records that SFE's management team is a General Manager and Chef, Aramark's is a Director, Chef, HR Manager and District Manager, and Chartwells' is a Director and Chef.

Chartwells outscored the others on several non-price items -- for example, it received full marks (7) for K-12 staffing experience, full points for expanding participation and promotional events, full points for administrative-review results, higher staffing-provision points, and 3 points for financial reporting where SFE and Aramark received 0. SFE and Aramark scored identically on most non-price rows.

The resulting totals are 83.00 for SFE, 74.33 for Aramark, and 84.81 for Chartwells. Although Chartwells submitted the highest per-meal price of the three, it earned the highest combined score, 84.81 out of 100, and is therefore the top-ranked bidder. This scoring rubric is the quantitative basis for the companion Food Service Contract Memo recommending award of the FSMC contract to Chartwells K12.

Background: Troy has partnered with an FSMC since 2009, beginning with Sodexo. By law, food-service contracts are renewed annually and must be competitively bid at least once every five years. Process: A selection committee used three evaluation tools -- a bid point calculator (price and non-price scoring rubric), an FY25 budget comparison for each bidder, and evaluation of cost-reimbursable addendums. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This memorandum, dated May 6, 2024, is from Gayle Moran, Food Service Liaison, to Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, and recommends award of the district's Food Service Management Company (FSMC) contract.

By way of background, the district began a partnership with an FSMC in 2009 with a contract with Sodexo. By law, food-service contracts must be renewed on an annual basis and must be competitively bid at least once every five years. As a result of the 2019 bid process, Chartwells K-12 was selected and has been the district's FSMC since. The current school year marks the milestone for another mandatory bid, which the district began planning earlier in the year by forming a selection committee of stakeholders from across the district. The formal bid process is heavily regulated by the Michigan Department of Education (MDE).

To assess the bids, the committee used three main evaluation tools: a bid point calculator (a scoring rubric measuring each bidder's price and non-price criteria, with emphasis on non-financial service aspects); an FY25 budget comparison for each bidder (projected revenues, all program costs, and a projected surplus/deficit); and an evaluation of the cost-reimbursable addendums contained in the proposals. Moran notes that comparing addendums is problematic because each is unique and does not allow an apples-to-apples comparison, and that the recommended FSMC's contract and addendum would be reviewed and approved by MDE and district legal counsel before Board consideration.

On March 21, 2024, the committee hosted a pre-bid meeting and walk-through at Troy High School (Stable Room, 2:00 pm); only management companies attending the pre-bid meeting could submit a proposal. Four companies attended: Chartwells K12, Aramark, Southwest Food Service Excellence LLC, and Taher, Inc. Sealed bids were received and opened on April 15, 2024 from three companies (SFE, Aramark, and Chartwells). On the scoring rubric, Chartwells K12 received the highest score of 84.81 out of 100, ahead of SFE at 83 and Aramark at 74.33.

The memo lays out a schedule of events: Bid Committee selected February 5, 2024; RFP sent to MDE February 20; RFP to be posted around March 18; pre-bid and walk-through March 21; vendor questions due April 1 with TSD responses April 2; addendums to MDE if necessary April 3; final sealed bids due April 15 by 2:00 pm; committee review of results April 16; final recommendation submitted to MDE April 17; proposed contract presented to the Board workshop May 7; contract to the Board for final approval May 21; board-approved contract sent to MDE May 22; and signed contract presented to the FSMC May 23.

Notable addendum items by bidder include: SFE's 'Cafe Refresh Decor' totaling $175,000; several Aramark provisions (a fee that can increase after year one if meal equivalents exceed the current rate cap, reimbursement of Aramark staff education and relocation costs and of its IT system, hold-harmless language requiring TSD legal scrutiny, a mismatch between the addendum's meal-equivalent count and the bid proposal, and a $160,000 investment for Aramark branding); and Chartwells' provision that management and administrative fees increase each year by CPI or 5%, whichever is less. The recommendation is to award the FSMC contract to Chartwells K12 for an initial term of one year with up to four one-year renewals, based on its highest combined score and its standing as the most financially responsible bidder in the budget comparison.

The recommendation followed a multi-year process that began with a 2022/2023 review of Grades 6-8 course structure and included a district Algebra 1 cohort and a 2023/2024 classroom pilot in which eight teachers vetted four curricula against a Math Curriculum Review Matrix. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented at the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop on May 7, 2024, this Teaching and Learning slide deck documents the district's Algebra 1 curriculum review and recommends adopting Illustrative Mathematics for Algebra 1 and Algebra 1 Honors.

Background ("Where We've Been, Grades 6-8"): In 2022/2023 the district conducted a full review of both course structure and curriculum for Grades 6-8. Stated lessons learned were to increase stakeholder communication and opportunities for input, begin earlier in the process with information and updates, expand grade levels, adopt a standardized assessment for long-term measurement of student progress, and consider what additional data is necessary.

Middle school implementation: The district hosted summer learning opportunities for teachers in August 2023, gave every teacher multiple opportunities for job-embedded learning with coaches, and held parent information and support nights at every middle school. It is currently piloting the NWEA standardized assessment for ongoing implementation support and updated the Teaching and Learning website. More than 500 student test-out opportunities were provided this spring. A parent information night featured Dr. Ted Coe on making the choice between Algebra 1 Honors and Math 8, and an algebra readiness assessment was given to all seventh graders as feedback for families.

Where we are, Algebra 1: An Algebra 1 cohort was established in 2022/2023, which reviewed potential resources, met with various publishers, and used the Math Curriculum Review Matrix to vet potential curricula. A Parent Information Night about the pilot was held in October 2023, math updates were communicated to all families through the Weekly Newsletter, and the cohort held monthly meetings to support the pilot. The district partnered with the Michigan Math and Science Network to embed 8th grade standards into Algebra 1 Honors.

Recommendation: The team investigated four curricula and narrowed to one using the District Review Matrix. College Preparatory Math (CPM) was judged out of date and due to be updated in the next year or two; Agile Mind was very technology heavy and difficult for teachers to be responsive; Open Up Resources (OUR) lacked a robust professional development structure; and Illustrative Mathematics (IM) was the recommended resource. Eight Algebra 1 and Algebra 1 Honors teachers participated in the pilot, implementing Illustrative Mathematics throughout the 2023/2024 school year, leading to the team recommendation of Illustrative Mathematics: Algebra 1.

Continued work and goals: to see growth in the number of students scoring advanced or proficient on the PSAT and SAT exams; to increase successful completion of Algebra 1 in 8th and/or 9th grade as measured through end-of-course summative exams and semester grades; and to build student problem-solving skills and communication of mathematical thinking as monitored through internal common assessments. Measurement of student achievement may include annually reported PSAT/SAT results (including cohort data) and NWEA math, along with unit and common assessments and student success (grades) in higher levels of mathematics studied with staff.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: An excerpt of Michigan's Revised School Code, Act 451 of 1976, Section 380.614 (MCL 380.614), which governs how intermediate school district (ISD) board members are elected. It provides that ISD board members are elected biennially on the first Monday in June by an electoral body of one representative designated by each constituent district's board, sets a six-year term, and specifies resolution, notice, nominating-petition signature, and $100 filing-fee requirements.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
- Statutory excerpt: The Revised School Code (Act 451 of 1976), Section 614, MCL 380.614, on election of intermediate school board members.

Election method
- Members elected biennially on the first Monday in June by an electoral body composed of one person designated by each constituent district board.
- Each constituent board designates its representative by resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days before the election, considered at not less than one public meeting, and adopted by majority vote; the resolution must identify the supported candidate(s) and direct the representative to vote for them at least on the first ballot.
- The ISD secretary sends certified-mail notice at least 10 days before the meeting, which is an open meeting under the Open Meetings Act (1976 PA 267).

Terms and vacancies
- Six-year term beginning July 1 after election; no more than two members from the same district (unless districts are fewer than seats).
- Vacancies filled by remaining members until the next biennial election; state board fills a vacancy not filled within 30 days.

Nomination
- Signature requirements: ISD population under 10,000 requires 6-20 signatures; population 10,000 or more requires 40-100.
- Petitions and affidavit (MCL 168.558) filed at least 30 days before the election; alternatively a $100 nonrefundable filing fee may be paid.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This document reproduces an excerpt of Michigan's Revised School Code, Act 451 of 1976, Section 614 (MCL 380.614), provided to constituent districts such as Troy in connection with the Oakland Schools ISD board election. The statute governs the election of intermediate school board members.

Subsection (1): Except as provided in section 615 and subject to section 642c of the Michigan election law (MCL 168.642c), members of the intermediate school board are elected biennially on the first Monday in June by an electoral body composed of one person designated by the board of each constituent school district.

Subsection (2): A constituent district's board designates its representative by resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days before the biennial election. The board must consider the resolution at not less than one public meeting before adopting it, and the resolution must be adopted by majority vote of the members serving on the board. The resolution must identify the candidate the board supports for each position and direct its representative to vote for that individual or individuals at least on the first ballot. The secretary of the intermediate school board sends notice by certified mail of the hour and place of the meeting to the secretary of each constituent board at least 10 days before the meeting. The president and secretary of the intermediate school board act as chairperson and secretary, and the meeting is an open meeting conducted under the Open Meetings Act, 1976 PA 267, MCL 15.261 to 15.275.

Subsection (3): Except as provided in section 703, each member's term of office is 6 years and begins on July 1 following election. Not more than 2 members of the intermediate school board may be from the same school district unless there are fewer districts than positions to be filled.

Subsection (4): A vacancy is filled by the remaining members until the next biennial election, when it is filled for the balance of the unexpired term. Notice of a vacancy is filed with the state board within 5 days; if not filled within 30 days, the vacancy is filled by the state board.

Subsections (5)-(6): A candidate must be nominated by petitions signed by school electors of the combined constituent districts. If the ISD population is less than 10,000 (most recent federal census), a minimum of 6 and maximum of 20 signatures are required; if 10,000 or more, a minimum of 40 and maximum of 100. A school elector may sign as many petitions as there are vacancies. Nominating petitions and an affidavit under section 558 of the Michigan election law (MCL 168.558) must be filed with the school district filing official not later than 30 days before the biennial election. The filing official determines the sufficiency of petitions and the eligibility of candidates and provides ballots listing all properly nominated candidates; the chairperson may accept floor nominations only if no petitions were filed for a vacancy.

Subsection (7): Instead of filing nominating petitions, a candidate may pay a nonrefundable $100.00 filing fee to the school district filing official; if paid by the petition due date, it has the same effect as filing petitions. The excerpt notes the statute's amendment history (1976 Act 451, with amendments through 2011 Act 232, effective Jan. 1, 2012).

These are the Oakland Intermediate School District (OISD / Oakland Schools) candidate guidelines for the Board of Education election, provided to constituent districts such as Troy. The election date is June 3, 2024, voters elect two members ("Vote for Two"), and each seat carries a six-year term ending June 30, 2030.

Filing official: The Oakland County Elections Division, West Wing Extension, 1st Floor, 1200 N. Telegraph Rd., Dept. 417, Pontiac, MI 48341-0417, phone (248) 858-0564.

Qualifications: A candidate for any seat on the Oakland Schools Board of Education must be a registered voter at least 18 years of age, a citizen of the United States, and must reside within one of Oakland County's school districts. Additionally, a candidate must be a resident of the State of Michigan for at least 30 days and a resident of one of the 28 constituent school districts on or before the 30th day prior to the election. For the 2024 election, a candidate may also be currently seated on a local school district board of education.

Nominating petitions, filing fee, and affidavits of identity: Friday, May 3, 2024 at 4:00 p.m. is the last day to file petitions with the County Clerk. Petition and Affidavit of Identity forms are available at the Oakland County Elections Division. A minimum of 40 and no more than 100 valid signatures is required for each candidate, and only qualified registered electors of the Oakland Intermediate School District may sign. Petitions must be circulated on a city/township basis, and electors may sign petitions for only as many candidates as there are persons to be elected. Those circulating petitions must be qualified registered electors in the State of Michigan; the circulator must sign each petition page and must date the form after it has been circulated. The County Clerk determines the sufficiency of petitions and the eligibility of candidates. A $100 nonrefundable fee may be filed by a candidate in lieu of a petition.

Conduct of meeting: The statutes governing OISD board elections through the meeting process provide that the chairperson may accept nominations for an available position from the floor only if no candidates filed for that position; where no candidate files, the ballot must contain several lines for hand entry of candidates nominated at the meeting. The President and Secretary of the OISD are responsible for convening and conducting any meetings held to fill board positions, and County Clerks are not required to play any role in the conduct of the meetings.

The email explains that Oakland Schools ISD Board members are elected by an electoral body composed of one person designated by the board of each constituent school district. Under the Revised School Code, each constituent board must adopt a resolution that designates a representative to vote on the district's behalf, directs the designee as to which candidates the board supports, and directs the designee to vote for those individuals at least on the first ballot. Designated electors must cast ballots in person at the election, scheduled 5:30-7:30 PM on Monday, June 3, 2024, at the Oakland Schools main campus, 2111 Pontiac Lake Road in Waterford; absentee ballots are prohibited. If a tie occurs, the district's designate or alternate must cast second and subsequent ballots in person during the hour after the announcement of results, and only districts whose designate or alternate appears in person will count toward the tiebreaking tally (a first-round ballot or supplied resolution does not carry to later rounds). Re-voting continues until the two candidates with the most votes are elected.

The email describes three historical options districts have used to satisfy the requirement to consider a resolution at no fewer than one meeting before adopting it: considering it as a discussion item at one open meeting and adopting it as an action item at a later open meeting on a separate date; considering it at one open meeting and adopting it at a second open meeting immediately following; or considering and adopting it at the same open meeting (with a recommendation to seek independent legal counsel confirming compliance). Resolutions must be adopted no earlier than 21 days before the election (on or after May 13, 2024) and a copy submitted to the Oakland Schools Superintendent's office via fax (248.209.2206) or email (nicole.christian@oakland.k12.mi.us) by 4:00 PM on Friday, May 31, 2024. Attached are the Revised School Code, a sample resolution template, and a revised election timeline reflecting the May 13-31 window; an official notice will be sent to each Board Secretary by certified mail.

Questions about the ISD board election process are directed to Sherry McMillan at 248.209.2062 or sherry.mcmillan@oakland.k12.mi.us. What it is
A suggested resolution (consent agenda item 5.E) for the Troy Board of Education to hold a statutorily required public hearing on the proposed 2024-2025 school-year budget.

Key decision
- A public hearing shall be held June 20, 2024 at 7:00 p.m. at a special Board meeting, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, to receive testimony and discuss the proposed 2024-2025 budget.
- The Board Secretary is authorized and directed to publish notice (substantially in the form of attached Exhibit A) in a newspaper of general circulation at least six days before the hearing.

Legal basis
- Michigan law requires each local unit of government, including a school district, to hold a public hearing on its proposed budget, with notice at least six days before.
- The notice must state the time and place and where the proposed budget is available for inspection, and must include, in 11-point bold face type: "THE PROPERTY TAX MILLAGE RATE PROPOSED TO BE LEVIED TO SUPPORT THE PROPOSED BUDGET WILL BE A SUBJECT OF THIS HEARING."

Exhibit A (notice text)
- Copies of the proposed budget available for inspection at the Administration Building, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Friday, June 14 through Thursday, June 20, 2024.
- Signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education.

Action
Recommended action: acceptance of the resolution; vote fields left blank.

The statutory provision further requires the notice to include, in 11-point bold face type, the statement: "THE PROPERTY TAX MILLAGE RATE PROPOSED TO BE LEVIED TO SUPPORT THE PROPOSED BUDGET WILL BE A SUBJECT OF THIS HEARING." The notice repeats the required 11-point bold-face millage-rate statement and is signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A spreadsheet workbook titled "Bid Point Calculator and Evaluation Criteria Matrix," attached as agenda item 5.F for the May 21, 2024 regular meeting, used by the Troy School District's food-service selection committee to score three competing Food Service Management Company (FSMC) bidders: SFE (Southwest Food Service Excellence), Aramark, and Chartwells.

Price scoring: Bidders entered a bid price per meal / meal equivalent, ranked lowest to highest: SFE at $2.906263, Aramark at $3.40028016, and Chartwells at $3.43. The calculator subtracts the lowest bid from each higher bid, divides by the lowest bid, subtracts the result from 1, and multiplies by 51 to yield bid points. SFE, as low bidder, received the full 51.00 price points; Aramark received 42.33; Chartwells received 41.81.

Non-price criteria: Up to 49 additional points were available across weighted categories, entered as evaluation points. Categories and select sub-criteria included: Management Candidate (7 pts for experience staffing K-12 breakfast and lunch programs, 2 pts for menu development and special events); Marketing & Merchandising Plan (expanding participation; promotions/promotional events); Nutrition Education (alternate low-fat/low-sodium offerings); Past Performance (results of Administrative Review; recent administrative/student/parent surveys); Plan of Operation (staffing recommendations; implementation of local wellness plan); Plan to Increase Participation (methods to obtain feedback; innovative service; alternate menu choices); District Specific Requirements (Point of Service systems, catering outside the district such as Head Start and Meals on Wheels, dietary accommodation, communication and relationships); District Manager Support (experience managing K-12 districts); Employee Training & Development (training programs, work safety, professional development for the on-site manager); Evaluation of FSMC References (relationship/communication, satisfaction, regulatory compliance); Integrity & Reliability of Projected Operating Budget (financial reports, 3 pts); and FSMC Guarantees (0 pts assigned).

Select scoring differences: On the 7-point K-12 staffing experience criterion, Chartwells scored 7 while SFE and Aramark each scored 4; Chartwells proposed a Director & Chef, SFE a General Manager & Chef, and Aramark a Director, Chef, HR Manager and District Manager. Chartwells earned 2 points each on expanding participation and on promotional events where both competitors scored 0, and 3 points on financial reports for revenue and cost where both competitors scored 0.

Totals: Adding price and non-price points, the workbook computes final scores out of 100: Chartwells 84.80930 (highest), SFE 83.00, and Aramark 74.33083. A summary sheet ("Sheet1") repeats these three totals. The results support the committee's recommendation to award the food-service management contract to Chartwells.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A May 6, 2024 memorandum from Food Service Liaison Gayle Moran to Deputy Superintendent Rick West recommending that the Troy School District award its food-service management contract to Chartwells K12 for an initial one-year term with up to four one-year renewals (agenda item 5.F). Chartwells scored highest at 84.81 of 100 on the committee's price and non-price rubric. The memo recounts the state-regulated bid process, four firms attended the March 21, 2024 pre-bid meeting and three (Chartwells, Aramark, SFE) submitted sealed bids opened April 15, 2024, and summarizes each bidder's cost-reimbursement addendums.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A memorandum (agenda item 5.F) dated May 6, 2024 from Gayle Moran, Food Service Liaison, to Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, recommending award of the district's Food Service Management Company (FSMC) contract to Chartwells K12.

Background
- The district began partnering with an FSMC in 2009 (Sodexo); Chartwells K-12 was selected in the 2019 bid and has served since.
- Michigan law requires annual contract renewal and a mandatory competitive bid at least every five years, making this a bid year.

Process and evaluation
- Three evaluation tools were used: a bid point calculator (price and non-price scoring), an FY25 budget comparison per bidder, and evaluation of cost-reimbursable addendums.
- Four firms attended the March 21, 2024 pre-bid meeting and walk-through at Troy High School: Chartwells K12, Aramark, Southwest Food Service Excellence LLC, and Taher, Inc.
- Sealed bids were opened April 15, 2024 from three firms; Chartwells scored highest at 84.81 of 100.

Addendum highlights
- SFE: included "Cafe Refresh Decor" totaling $175,000.
- Aramark: fee-increase clause tied to meal equivalents; reimbursable staff education/relocation and IT-system costs; hold-harmless modifications; a meal-equivalent discrepancy; and $160,000 for branding.
- Chartwells: management and administrative fees increase annually by CPI or 5%, whichever is less.

Recommendation
Award to Chartwells K12 for an initial one-year term with up to four one-year renewals, subject to MDE and legal-counsel review.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum attached as agenda item 5.F for the May 21, 2024 regular meeting, dated May 6, 2024, from Gayle Moran, Food Service Liaison, to Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, titled "Food Service Management Contract Bid Award Recommendation."

Background: The district began a partnership with a Food Service Management Company (FSMC) in 2009 under a contract with Sodexo. By law, food-service contracts must be renewed annually and mandatorily bid at least once every five years. The 2019 bid process selected Chartwells K-12, which has been the district's FSMC since. The current year marked another mandatory bid, planned earlier in the year with a selection committee of district stakeholders and conducted under a schedule heavily regulated by the Michigan Department of Education (MDE).

Evaluation tools: The committee used three tools: (1) a bid point calculator, a scoring rubric measuring each bidder's price and non-price criteria, emphasizing non-financial service aspects; (2) an FY25 budget comparison for each bidder incorporating projected revenues, costs, and a projected surplus/deficit; and (3) evaluation of cost-reimbursable addendums proposing changes to the contract related to cost reimbursement (noted as difficult to compare "apples to apples").

Bid process: On March 21, 2024 the committee hosted a pre-bid meeting and walk-through; only companies attending could submit proposals. Four companies attended: Chartwells K12, Aramark, Southwest Food Service Excellence LLC, and Taher, Inc. Bids were received and opened April 15, 2024 from three companies. Chartwells K12 received the highest score, 84.81 out of 100 possible points.

Process timeline (selected dates): Bid Committee selected February 5, 2024; RFP sent to MDE February 20, 2024; pre-bid and walk-through at the THS Stable Room March 21, 2024 at 2:00 pm; vendor questions due April 1, 2024; final sealed bids due April 15, 2024 by 2:00 pm; committee review April 16; final recommendation submitted to MDE April 17; proposed contract presented to the Board workshop May 7, 2024; contract to the Board for final approval May 21, 2024; board-approved contract to MDE May 22; signed contract to the FSMC May 23, 2024.

Addendum summary by bidder: SFE included "Cafe Refresh Decor" totaling $175,000. Aramark included a clause allowing its fee to increase after year one if meal equivalents rise more than the current rate cap, reimbursement for staff education and relocation costs and for the cost of its IT system, hold-harmless language modifications requiring legal scrutiny, a discrepancy between the number of meal equivalents in the addendum versus the bid proposal, and a $160,000 investment for Aramark branding. Chartwells provided that management and administrative fees shall increase each year by CPI or 5%, whichever is less.

Recommendation: Based on the rubric (12 criteria scoring Chartwells highest on price and non-price criteria) and the budget comparison (identifying Chartwells as the most financially responsible bidder), Moran recommends awarding the food-service management contract to Chartwells K12 for an initial term of one year, with up to four one-year renewals. Any recommended FSMC contract and addendum would be reviewed and approved by MDE and the district's legal counsel before Board consideration.

Eight Algebra 1 and Algebra 1 Honors teachers piloted the resource throughout 2023/2024; it was chosen over College Preparatory Math (CPM), Agile Mind, and Open Up Resources. The presentation also recaps grades 6-8 implementation, including summer 2023 teacher training, NWEA assessment piloting, over 500 student test-outs, and parent information nights, and sets goals tied to PSAT/SAT growth and Algebra 1 completion in 8th or 9th grade.

What it is

- 2022/2023: full review of course structure and curriculum for grades 6-8.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A slide presentation attached as agenda item 7.A for the Troy Board of Education's May 21, 2024 regular meeting, documenting the district's multi-year secondary mathematics review and recommending an Algebra 1 curriculum adoption.

Where we've been (Grades 6-8): In 2022/2023 the district conducted a full review of both course structure and curriculum for grades 6-8. Lessons learned included the need to increase stakeholder communication and opportunities for input, to begin earlier with information and updates, to expand grade-level messaging for students immediately impacted and those who may be impacted in subsequent years, to adopt an additional standardized assessment for long-term measurement of student progress, and to consider what additional data is necessary.

Middle school implementation: The district hosted summer learning opportunities for teachers in August 2023; every teacher has had multiple opportunities for job-embedded learning with coaches; parent information and support nights were held at every middle school; the NWEA standardized assessment is being piloted for ongoing implementation support; the Teaching and Learning website was updated; over 500 student test-out opportunities were provided this spring; a parent information night was held with Dr. Ted Coe on making the choice between Algebra 1 Honors and Math 8; and an algebra readiness assessment was given to all seventh graders as feedback for families.

Algebra 1 review: An Algebra 1 cohort was established in 2022/2023, which reviewed potential resources, met with various publishers, and used the Math Curriculum Review Matrix to vet curricula. A Parent Information Night about the pilot was held in October 2023, district communication went to all families on math updates via the Weekly Newsletter, monthly Algebra 1 Cohort meetings supported the pilot, and the district partnered with the Michigan Math and Science Network to embed 8th-grade standards into Algebra 1 Honors.

Recommendation: The team investigated four curricula and narrowed to one using the District Review Matrix. College Preparatory Math (CPM) was judged out of date and due to be updated in the next year or two; Agile Mind was very technology-heavy and difficult for teachers to be responsive; Open Up Resources (OUR) lacked a robust professional-development structure; and Illustrative Mathematics (IM) was the recommended resource. Eight Algebra 1 and Algebra 1 Honors math teachers participated in the pilot, implementing Illustrative Mathematics throughout the 2023/2024 school year, leading to the team recommendation of Illustrative Mathematics: Algebra 1.

Continued work and goals: The stated goals are to see growth in the number of students scoring advanced or proficient on the PSAT and SAT exams; to increase successful completion of Algebra 1 in 8th and/or 9th grade as measured through end-of-course summative exams and semester grades; and to build student problem-solving skills and communication of mathematical thinking as monitored through internal common assessment. Measurement of student achievement may include annually reported PSAT/SAT (including cohort data), exploratory NWEA math, and unit and common assessments studied with staff, along with student success (grades) in higher levels of mathematics.

Oakland Schools is one of 56 Intermediate School Districts (ISDs) established in Michigan in 1962; it is an autonomous, tax-supported public school district governed by Michigan General School Law that provides regional service to constituent local districts, of which Troy is one. Its stated mission is "Oakland Schools: Learning today. Transforming tomorrow," and the summary lays out beliefs and direction emphasizing service, student achievement, collaboration, stewardship of public resources and ethical behavior.

How it is funded: proposed total funding for FY2024-25 is $470.0 million, comprising property taxes of $249.5 million, other local revenue and investment revenue of $44.5 million, state source revenue of $23.2 million, other financing sources and indirect revenue of $20.7 million, and estimated grant award funding of $132.1 million. What is new or significant: property tax revenue is budgeted to increase 5.8%, or $13.7 million. Taxable values have increased incrementally over the last eleven years and have finally reached pre-recession levels; while Oakland County taxable values are expected to grow more than 6.0%, the District used a conservative estimate pending actual values. Tax abatements have leveled off after peaking in fiscal years 2012 and 2013, though the full economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic remains undetermined and the environment is described as ripe for an increase in tax-tribunal challenges, for which the District holds reserves. All winners were forwarded to Oakland Schools to represent Troy in the countywide Outstanding Teacher Award program. The agenda also included a Mission Moment on Autism Acceptance Month, a Student Spotlight, and Volunteer Appreciation.

Under recognition of Autism Acceptance Month, the Board took up a resolution to celebrate the contributions of all neurodiverse people and to work toward ending disparities that autistic people experience in accessing employment, healthcare and education. The motion was made by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Alic. The recorded resolution recites that Autism Spectrum Disorder affects more than five million people in the United States; that the CDC reports 1 in 36 children may have autism; that autism is a neurological and developmental disorder characterized by social impairment and restricted interactive and communication behaviors that can affect anyone regardless of race, ethnicity, gender or socioeconomic background; that symptoms present in varied combinations and can create lifelong challenges; that a range of professionals, including physicians, psychologists, behavior analysts, speech and language pathologists, occupational therapists, vocational rehabilitation professionals and educators, can assist through early identification, education and intervention; and that the Troy School District is committed to fostering acceptance and belonging. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is: A consent-agenda item (5.D) for the May 21, 2024 regular meeting -- consideration to approve/support the Oakland Intermediate School District (OISD) 2024-2025 General Fund budget.

Statutory basis: Section 624 of Michigan's Revised School Code, as amended, requires the intermediate school board to submit its proposed General Fund budget to each constituent district no later than May 1 each year. By June 1, each constituent district's board must review the proposed budget, adopt a resolution expressing support or disapproval, and submit any specific objections and proposed changes to the intermediate board.

Board action: The recommended action is to adopt the resolution. Its operative terms state that the board has received and reviewed the proposed OISD General Fund budget under Section 624 and expresses support for it; direct the board secretary (or designee) to forward a copy to the intermediate school board or its superintendent no later than June 1; and rescind any conflicting prior resolutions.

Format: Drafted as a motion, with blanks for the moving and supporting members and for Yes/No vote tallies, followed by a declaration of adoption.

Certification: A Secretary's certification block attests the text is a true and complete copy of a resolution adopted at the regular meeting held May 21, 2024, part of the board's minutes, with public notice given under the Open Meetings Act (1976 PA 267, as amended).

Purpose: Record Troy's statutory support for its intermediate district's budget and satisfy the June 1 review-and-response obligation. No OISD dollar figures appear in the document itself.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy Board of Education's consent agenda for its regular meeting on May 21, 2024 included Item 5.D, a consideration to approve the Oakland Intermediate School District (OISD) 2024-2025 budget. The action rests on Section 624 of Michigan's Revised School Code, as amended, which governs how an intermediate school district's budget is reviewed by its constituent local districts.

The resolution recites two statutory premises. First, Section 624 requires the intermediate school board to submit its proposed General Fund budget no later than May 1 of each year to the board of each constituent district for review. Second, not later than June 1 of each year, the board of each constituent district must review the proposed intermediate school district General Fund budget, adopt a board resolution expressing its support for or disapproval of the proposed budget, and submit to the intermediate school board any specific objections and proposed changes it has.

The operative resolution provides that: (1) the board of education has received and reviewed the proposed intermediate school district General Fund budget in accordance with Section 624 and, by adopting the resolution, expresses its support for the proposed budget; (2) the secretary of the board of education or a designee shall forward a copy of the resolution to the intermediate school board or its superintendent no later than June 1; and (3) all resolutions in conflict with this resolution are rescinded.

The document is formatted as a motion, with blank lines for the members who move and support it, blank Yes and No tallies, and a line noting the resolution was declared adopted. It concludes with a certification block in which the undersigned, duly qualified and acting Secretary of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, Michigan, certifies that the foregoing is a true and complete copy of a resolution adopted by the Board of Education at a regular meeting held May 21, 2024, that the original is a part of the board's minutes, and that notice of the meeting was given to the public under the Open Meetings Act, 1976 PA 267, as amended.

The document contains no dollar amounts for the OISD budget; it is the procedural instrument by which Troy formally records its support and meets the statutory review-and-response deadline of June 1.

Budget presentation delivered at the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop on June 6, 2024 (title slide dated June 20, 2024), addressing three areas: Truth-in-Taxation and establishment of millage rates, the 2023-24 Final Budget Amendment, and the 2024-25 Proposed Budget.

Taxable values and millage rates: Total taxable value increased 6.80%, from $5,009,975,860 in 2023 to $5,350,643,690 in 2024. Homestead value rose to $3,490,317,132 and non-homestead to $1,860,326,558. The five-year homestead millage comparison shows a constant 6.0000 State Education Tax (S.E.T.), a declining hold-harmless levy (4.6750 in 2020/21 falling to a proposed 2.7294 in 2024/25), a debt levy rising to 6.1000, and a sinking fund of 0.9606. Non-homestead property carries the statutory 18.0000 mills plus S.E.T. and debt, for a proposed 2024/25 total of about 31.0606 mills versus roughly 15.2706 on homestead property. The L-4029 tax rate request form is referenced.

2023-24 General Fund budget amendment (Amendment 1 versus Amendment 3 recommended): Total revenues were revised down $526,839 to $193,048,749, with Local Sources up $329,819 to $44,487,819, State Sources down $357,018 to $128,542,649, Federal Sources down $10,214 to $7,900,438, and Interdistrict Sources down $489,426 to $12,117,843. Total expenditures rose $1,452,944 to $190,748,491, with notable changes in Purchased Services (up $768,390 to $24,880,176), Payments to Other Districts (up $270,000 to $1,668,900), Other (up $191,705 to $466,769), and Debt Service (down $128,690 to $475,400). The net change in fund balance fell from $4,280,041 to $2,300,258; beginning fund balance was $32,620,321 and the projected ending balance $34,920,579, or 18.31% (down from 19.49%).

2024-25 Proposed Budget: Projected total revenues of $191,544,523, down $1,504,226 (-0.8%). Local Sources rise $2,967,526 (+6.7%) to $47,455,345 on higher property values (offset by declining investment revenue); State Sources fall $2,106,561 (-1.6%) to $126,436,088; Federal Sources drop $3,398,433 (-43.0%) to $4,502,005; and Interdistrict Sources rise $1,033,242 (+8.5%) to $13,151,085. Salaries increase $3,206,055 (+3.65%) to $90,976,772. Key assumptions include an enrollment projection of 12,300 (down 70), a foundation allowance increase of $241 per pupil (Governor's budget), final reductions in Section 20f funding, a $1.4 million material reduction in Section 31aa funding, a $3.0 million ESSER Equalization (Section 11t) reduction, a retirement effective-rate increase, the PA 152 health-insurance hard cap effective January 1, 2024, and inclusion of the 2024-25 obligation for TLC debt. The narrative frames these under themes of federal funding decline, enrollment, structural budget, staff alignment, and strategic use of fund balance.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
"Project 2026 Blueprint" Accountability Plan presentation delivered to the Troy School District (TSD) Board of Education Workshop on June 6, 2024. The plan is framed around the district's "World Class for All" strategy, which holds the team accountable through four color-coded pillars, each reported in terms of Objectives, Key Results, and Challenges & Recommendations for June 2024.

Blue Pillar - Deep Learning: Objectives include creating and sustaining multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS) that deepen learning and empower student voice, improving technology access, pursuing global best practices, and upgrading facilities. Key results cite partnerships with New Solutions K-12 (student supports K-12), Solution Tree (PLC model, grades 6-12), and Oakland Schools (MTSS); development of an Artificial Intelligence leadership committee and a computer science leadership team; growth of student digital portfolios; use of NPDL and "The 6 C's"; hosting the Midwest Literacy Institute; and Math Recovery K-12. Facilities work references Fielding International's comprehensive guiding principles for middle and high school redesign and ongoing bond project work. Challenges include monitoring benchmark data, developing math capacity, and solidifying tier-one instruction.

Gold Pillar - Building Capacity: Objectives focus on improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators, providing job-embedded professional learning, and co-designing experiences for the "OneTroy" community. Key results include attending university job fairs, "Grow Your Own" programs, employee support groups, a Leadership Cohort, and a New Teacher Learning Series; a continued partnership with Celebrate Hope; community engagement (Community Book Read and Experience Panel); and student-capacity programs WEB, LEAP, and a Student Leadership Conference, plus Learning Nights at all schools. The teacher shortage and limited university education enrollment are named as challenges.

Red Pillar - Equity and Well-Being: Objectives are to fund investments supporting the needs of the whole child and to elevate Alignment, Access, and Agency district-wide. Key results include SEL curriculum and programming, a Behavioral Threat Assessment (BTA) committee, a Belonging Survey, expansion of the Student Equity Council, and building an inclusive calendar with community input. Recommendations emphasize restorative practices (training all administrators, growing building cohorts), district training on a new BTA tool, and "Belonging as a System" (inclusive newsletter, data culture, professional learning, resources for honoring diversity).

Green Pillar - Early Childhood to Career: The objective is continued investment in high-quality early childhood education, including advocacy for universal preschool access for all three- and four-year-olds. Key results cite increased Great Start Readiness Program (GSRP) slots for 2024-25, the personalized transition of 326 students into TSD kindergarten, and continued connection to the TSD K-5 curriculum. (The extracted text is truncated within the Green Pillar section.)

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Minutes and resolution from a special meeting of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, held June 6, 2024 at 5:00 p.m. The document is the "Resolution Certifying Operating Millage Renewal Proposal," which places an operating-millage renewal question before district voters.

Background (WHEREAS clauses): The Board determined it is necessary for continued operation of the district to renew authority to levy certain operating mills and to increase prior authority to protect against future Headlee Amendment rollbacks, as described in the Operating Millage Renewal Proposal attached as Exhibit A. The measure is to be submitted at an election on November 5, 2024, and must be certified to the Clerk of Oakland County (the "School District Election Coordinator") no later than 4:00 p.m. on August 13, 2024, as required by Michigan election law.

Resolved provisions: (1) The Exhibit A proposal is certified to the Election Coordinator and local clerks for the November election, with the Board Secretary and the Superintendent each authorized to file the resolution and any required forms by the August 13 deadline. (2) The Secretary or Superintendent may update the proposal before submission to reflect any Headlee rollbacks applicable to the current operating millage for 2024. (3) The Election Coordinator is directed to post and publish notices of the last day of registration and of the election and to prepare ballots in the Exhibit A form. (4) Conflicting prior resolutions are rescinded. The resolution records YES and NO member lines and is "RESOLUTION DECLARED ADOPTED," certified by Gary Hauff, Secretary of the Board of Education, with an attestation of compliance with the Open Meetings Act (Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976).

Exhibit A - Operating Millage Renewal Proposal (ballot language): The proposal would renew the district's authority, which expires with the 2025 tax levy, to levy up to 18.00 mills for general school district operating purposes on taxable property not exempt from the levy; restrict the levy on principal residences (owner-occupied homes) to no more than 5.7049 mills; and protect against Headlee rollbacks of up to 4.0 mills. This would allow the district to continue levying the statutory 18.00 mills on non-homestead property (principally industrial and commercial real property and residential rental property) and to levy on principal residences only the portion of mills necessary to receive the full per-pupil foundation allowance permitted by the State. The document notes the district levied only 2.7936 mills on personal residences (owner-occupied homes) in 2024. The ballot question asks whether the limitation on taxes may be increased by 22 mills - with 18 mills the maximum allowable levy ($18.00 per $1,000 of taxable value), of which not more than 5.7049 mills may be imposed on principal residences - for twenty (20) years, the years 2026 to 2045 inclusive, to provide funds for operating expenses. If approved and levied, the millage is estimated to generate approximately $42.5 million during the 2026 calendar year for general operating purposes.

What it is:
The standard MHSAA Membership Resolution that a district's governing board adopts annually to enroll its secondary schools in the Michigan High School Athletic Association and its sanctioned tournaments. This copy is for the 2024-25 membership year.

Key terms:
- Effective August 1, 2024 through July 31, 2025; may not be revoked during that period.
- Enrolls the district's junior high/middle and senior high schools as MHSAA members and to participate in approved interschool athletic activities.
- Delegates supervision and control of those activities to the Superintendent or designee.
- Adopts the MHSAA Constitution, By-Laws, and Handbook rules, regulations, and interpretations as minimum standards, with agreement to primary enforcement.
- Schools hosting or participating in MHSAA meets/tournaments must follow all tournament policies and meet Regulation I minimums and Regulation II maximums.

Eligibility note:
Member school buildings must have enrollment and onsite attendance of at least 15 students (grades 6-8/9 or 9/10-12); nonpublic schools must be tax-exempt not-for-profits.

Administrative details:
MHSAA is a voluntary nonprofit at 1661 Ramblewood Drive, East Lansing, MI 48823, (517) 332-5046. Completed resolutions are returned to camala@mhsaa.com. Resolutions modified or conditioned in any way are rejected.

The Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) Membership Resolution form for the 2024-25 membership year, which a school district's Board of Education must formally ratify to enroll its secondary schools in the association. The resolution states that the listed junior high/middle and senior high schools under the board's direction, located in a named city/township and county in Michigan, are (A) enrolled as members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association, Inc., a nonprofit association, and (B) further enrolled to participate in the approved interschool athletic activities the association sponsors.

By adopting it, the Board of Education/Governing Body delegates to the Superintendent or designee(s) responsibility for the supervision and control of those athletic activities, accepts the association's Constitution and By-Laws, and adopts the rules, regulations, and interpretations published in the current Handbook as minimum standards and the governing code for its interscholastic athletics program, agreeing to primary enforcement. Schools that host or participate in the association's meets and tournaments must follow and enforce all tournament policies, procedures, and schedules, and must adhere to at least the minimum standards of Regulation I and the maximum limitations of Regulation II in all MHSAA tournament sports.

The authorization is effective from August 1, 2024 and remains effective until July 31, 2025, during which period it may not be revoked. The form includes a Record of Adoption block for the governing body name, board secretary (or designee) signature, address, city and ZIP, contact e-mail, and the meeting date of adoption.

Supporting text explains that MHSAA is a voluntary nonprofit corporation of public, private, and parochial junior high/middle and senior high schools, headquartered at 1661 Ramblewood Drive, East Lansing, MI 48823, (517) 332-5046. Member school buildings must have enrollment and onsite attendance of at least 15 students (for grade configurations such as 6-8/9, 7-8/9, or 9/10-12); nonpublic schools must qualify for federal income-tax exemption as not-for-profit organizations, and schools may join at the 6th-grade level to reach the 15-student minimum. Completed resolutions are to be saved and e-mailed as an attachment to camala@mhsaa.com. The instructions warn that resolutions modified in any way, or supplemented with letters placing additional conditions on membership or tournament participation, will be rejected.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A resolution presented for adoption at the June 20, 2024 meeting in which the Troy School District Board of Education expresses support for gun safety and safe firearm storage. Citing statistics that firearms are the leading cause of death among U.S. children and adolescents and that most school-attack firearms come from a parent's or relative's home, it directs the Superintendent to communicate the importance of secure firearm storage during Gun Violence Awareness Month and in annual notification materials, and to keep working with law enforcement, health, and nonprofit partners. It is certified by board secretary Gary N. Hauff.

What it is:
A resolution (agenda item 3.C) for adoption at the June 20, 2024 meeting: the Troy School District Board of Education's Resolution in Support of Gun Safety and Safe Gun Storage.

Key findings cited (WHEREAS):
- Firearms are the leading cause of death among U.S. children and adolescents.
- Firearm death rates for ages 14-17 are 22.5% higher than motor-vehicle death rates.
- Per the U.S. Secret Service, 76% of school attackers obtained a firearm from a parent's or relative's home.
- Roughly 350 children under 18 unintentionally shoot themselves or others each year.
- Nearly 22,000 Americans die by firearm suicide annually, including 950+ children and teens.
- 47% of gun owners with children do not securely store at least one weapon.

- The Superintendent will periodically communicate safe-storage importance during Gun Violence Awareness Month and include it in annual notification materials.
- The Board and Superintendent will keep working with local law enforcement, medical/mental-health agencies, and nonprofits to inform parents about secure storage.
- The resolution shall not be construed to conflict with Michigan or federal law.

Certified by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education, under the Open Meetings Act (Act 267, P.A. 1976). YES/NO vote lines are left blank in this copy.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A resolution (agenda item 3.C) placed before the Troy School District Board of Education at its June 20, 2024 regular meeting, titled "Resolution in Support of Gun Safety and Safe Gun Storage." The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution.

The preamble sets out a series of WHEREAS findings: that the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and staff is a top district priority; that firearm-related death is the leading cause of death among children and adolescents; that firearm death rates among ages 14 to 17 are now 22.5% higher than motor-vehicle-related death rates, making firearm injury the leading single cause of death for middle- and high-school-age children; that, per a U.S. Secret Service report, in incidents of gun violence on school grounds 76% of attackers acquired a firearm from the home of a parent or another close relative; that roughly 350 children under 18 unintentionally shoot themselves or someone else each year; that nearly 22,000 Americans die by firearm suicide annually, including over 950 children and teens; that research indicates 47% of firearm owners with children in the home do not safely store at least one weapon; and that secure firearm storage is an essential component of keeping the community safe.

The operative clauses resolve that the Board directs the Superintendent to periodically communicate the importance of safe firearm storage and other firearm-safety and violence-prevention measures during gun violence awareness month, and to disseminate material annually stressing secure firearm storage by including it in the district's annual notification materials. A further clause commits the Board and Superintendent to continue working with local law enforcement agencies, medical and mental-health agencies, and nonprofit organizations to inform district parents of their obligations regarding secure firearm storage and other gun-violence-prevention measures. A final clause states the resolution shall not be construed to conflict with any existing Michigan or federal law.

The document includes YES and NO vote lines (left blank in this copy) and a certification, signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary of the Board of Education, attesting that the resolution was duly adopted at the regular meeting held June 20, 2024 in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act (Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976). The resolution cites supporting sources including University of Michigan / Michigan Medicine analyses, the U.S. Secret Service report "Protecting America's Schools," Everytown Research, Pew Research Center, and a 2005 JAMA study by David C. Grossman et al. on gun-storage practices and youth suicide and unintentional firearm injury risk.

The operative resolution states that the Troy Board of Education appoints Natalie Haezebrouck and members of the Teaching and Learning Department as representatives of the districtwide Professional Development Advisory Committee. The recommended action is to accept the resolution; Yes/No vote lines are left blank in this copy.

The item explains the statutory backdrop under State School Aid Act Section 101(10): districts seeking to count professional development toward required instructional hours must ensure that "qualifying" professional development aligns with the school or district improvement plan under which it is provided; links to one or more criteria of the district's teacher evaluation tool; is approved by the Michigan Department of Education (MDE) as counting for State Continuing Education Clock Hours (SCECHs); is not more than ten combined hours occurring before the first scheduled day of school and after the last scheduled day of school; is not more than ten hours in a single month; and includes in attendance at least 75% of the teachers who were scheduled to participate. Establishing the advisory committee supports the district's compliance with these requirements.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This Food Service Department memorandum, dated June 11, 2024, is from Gayle Moran, Food Service Liaison, to Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, regarding 'Equipment Purchases for Spend Down Plan.' It explains that the district's Food Service Account currently holds an excess of funds - as determined by the Michigan Department of Education (MDE) - and that these funds will be used to improve and/or replace equipment within the Food Service Department.

The specific recommendation is to replace the serving counters at Boulan Middle School, Larson Middle School, and Wass Elementary with equipment previously approved by MDE. The memo notes that all included items are portable components of the serving line. Quotes were requested for the entire serving line at all three schools through the district's approved MOR Commodity & Commercial Food Purchasing Cooperative. One quote was received, from Stafford-Smith, Inc.; of the two other cooperative members contacted, one relinquished its opportunity to bid because it was out of state, and the third did not respond within the allotted timeframe.

Moran therefore recommends awarding the total purchase of $317,179.00 to Stafford-Smith, Inc., allocated as follows: Boulan Middle School $131,529.00, Larson Middle School $131,883.00, and Wass Elementary $53,767.00. A copy of the Stafford-Smith, Inc. quote and detailed specifications is attached to the memo for review. The memo cautions that availability and delivery of the equipment may not take place until later in September.

The purchase will be funded by the Food Service Fund, and the memo emphasizes that the items are all on the approved replacement list maintained by the Michigan Department of Education. The document is part of the June 20, 2024 regular Board of Education meeting packet and represents one of two food-service spend-down equipment recommendations Moran submitted for that meeting, the other covering replacement UNOX ovens at International Academy-East, Larson, and Smith.

- Existing ovens at IA-East, Larson MS, and Smith MS are non-repairable; the recommendation is to replace them with double-stack gas UNOX ovens, cited as reliable and multi-functional for increased production needs.

Procurement
- Three quotes were received; Gold Star Products was lowest at $90,589.75.

Recommended purchase - Gold Star Products
- International Academy-East: $31,822.05
- Larson MS: $31,822.04
- Smith MS: $31,822.04
- Gas Connector Kits: $1,950.00
- Less allowable trade-in and energy rebates: $(6,826.38)
- Net total: $90,589.75

Funded by the Food Service Fund; items are on the MDE approved replacement list. A Gold Star Products quote and a three-quote cost comparison are attached.

To justify the recommendation behind the oven-replacement resolution (item 9.B).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This Food Service Department memorandum, dated June 11, 2024, is from Gayle Moran, Food Service Liaison, to Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, regarding 'Equipment Purchases for Spend Down Plan.' It states that the district's Food Service Account currently holds an excess of funds - as determined by the Michigan Department of Education (MDE) - which will be used to improve and/or replace equipment within the Food Service Department.

The recommendation is to replace the existing, non-repairable ovens at IA-East (International Academy-East), Larson Middle School, and Smith Middle School with double-stack gas UNOX ovens. The memo notes these ovens have proven reliable and offer multiple functions that provide greater efficiency in meeting the district's increased production needs.

Three quotes were received, with Gold Star Products submitting the lowest at $90,589.75. Moran therefore recommends awarding the purchase to Gold Star Products, itemized as: International Academy-East $31,822.05, Larson MS $31,822.04, and Smith MS $31,822.04, plus Gas Connector Kits at $1,950.00, less allowable trade-in and energy rebates of $6,826.38 - netting to the $90,589.75 total. A copy of the Gold Star Products quote and the cost comparison of the three submitted quotes are attached for review.

The purchase will be funded by the Food Service Fund, and the memo notes the items are on the approved replacement list with the MDE. This memorandum is the supporting justification for agenda item 9.B ('Replacement Ovens - IAE, Larson, Smith') at the June 20, 2024 regular Board of Education meeting, whose suggested resolution awards the three-oven UNOX purchase to Gold Star Products for $90,589.75 from the Food Service Fund. It is one of two spend-down equipment memoranda Moran submitted for that meeting; the other recommends serving-line replacements at Boulan, Larson, and Wass through Stafford-Smith, Inc.

Taxable values and millage
- 2024 total taxable value $5,350,643,690, up 6.80% from $5,009,975,860 (homestead $3.49B; non-homestead $1.86B).

2023-24 amendment (Amendment 3)

- Total expenditures $192,248,491 (up $2,952,944, or 1.6%), led by salaries of $89,270,717.

Proposed 2024-25 budget
- Total revenues $191,544,523 (down 0.8%); federal sources fall 43% ($3,398,433) as ESSER (11t) ends.
- Local sources rise 6.7% to $47,455,345; salaries $90,976,772; benefits $67,671,683.
- Assumptions: enrollment 12,300 (down 70), foundation allowance +$241/pupil, a $1.4M reduction in 31aa funding, PA 152 health-insurance hard cap, and TLC debt service.

To inform the Board's adoption of 2024 millage rates and the annual budget amendment and appropriation.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Prepared by Troy School District's Business Services division for the Board of Education's June 20, 2024 regular meeting, this presentation combines three items: the annual Truth-in-Taxation hearing and establishment of millage rates (documented on State Form L-4029), a final amendment to the 2023-24 General Fund budget, and the proposed 2024-25 General Fund budget.

Taxable values: 2024 homestead taxable value is $3,490,317,132 (up from $3,286,622,690) and non-homestead is $1,860,326,558 (up from $1,723,353,170), for a total of $5,350,643,690 - a 6.80% increase over 2023's $5,009,975,860. Five-year millage tables show the proposed 2024/25 homestead levy at 15.2706 mills (S.E.T. 6.0000, Hold Harmless 2.7294, Debt 6.1000, Sinking Fund 0.9606) versus 15.8415 the prior year, and non-homestead at 31.0606 mills (adding the 18.0000 statewide levy). The Debt levy had risen from 4.1000 to 6.1000 mills between 2022/23 and 2023/24.

2023-24 General Fund amendment: revenues by source were revised to Local $44,487,819, State $128,542,649, Federal $7,900,438, and Interdistrict $12,117,843, totaling $193,048,749 - a $526,839 decrease, driven largely by a $489,426 (3.9%) drop in interdistrict (PA-18) revenue. Expenditures rose to $192,248,491 (up $2,952,944, 1.6%): Salaries $89,270,717 (+$1,709,046), Employee Benefits $66,143,373, Purchased Services $24,880,176 (+$768,390), Repairs and Maintenance $1,519,120, Supplies and Materials $6,893,367, Capital Outlay $930,669, Debt Service $475,400 (-21.3%), Other $466,769 (+69.7%), and Payments to Other Districts $1,668,900 (+$270,000). The net change in fund balance fell from a budgeted $4,280,041 to $800,258; beginning fund balance was $32,620,321 and ending balance $33,420,579, or 17.38% (down from a projected 19.49%).

Proposed 2024-25 budget: revenues total $191,544,523 (down $1,504,226, 0.8%). Local sources rise 6.7% to $47,455,345 on higher property values (offset by declining investment revenue); State sources fall 1.6% to $126,436,088; Federal sources drop 43.0% to $4,502,005 on a $3.0 million ESSER Equalization (11t) reduction; Interdistrict rises 8.5% to $13,151,085. Expenditures include Salaries $90,976,772 (+1.91%), Employee Benefits $67,671,683 (+2.31%), Purchased Services $24,805,176, and Repairs and Maintenance $1,454,120. Key assumptions: enrollment projected at 12,300 (down 70), a Governor's-budget foundation allowance increase of $241 per pupil, final section 20f reductions, a $1.4 million cut in 31aa funding, a retirement effective-rate increase, the PA 152 health-insurance hard cap effective January 1, 2024, and debt service including the 2024-25 TLC obligation. The document supports the Board's adoption of millage rates and the year-end budget amendment and 2024-25 appropriation.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An award packet from the Association of School Business Officials International (ASBO International), dated April 18, 2024, informing the Troy School District that it has received ASBO's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting (COE). The certificate states that it is presented to Troy School District for its Annual Comprehensive Financial Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2023, having met the criteria established for ASBO International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting. It is signed by Ryan S. Stechschulte, President, and James M. Rowan, CAE, SFO, CEO/Executive Director.

A cover letter from James M. Rowan is addressed to Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois (rendered Livermois in the letter), Troy, MI 48098. It congratulates the district, describes the award as a significant achievement reflecting a commitment to transparency and high-quality financial reporting, and encourages use of the COE recipient logo. The letter advises that the COE Review Team has provided comments for improving the district's ACFR, that those comments should be addressed before the next report, and that the district must include the original comments and its written responses in the following year's application packet. The award certificate and a press release are attached.

The attached press release carries the dateline Ashburn, VA - April 18, 2024, with media contact Allison Barton-Kramer, and is headlined that the school district was awarded for outstanding financial reporting. It quotes ASBO International Executive Director Jim Rowan, CAE, SFO, stating that for over half a century the Certificate of Excellence has been the gold standard in promoting and recognizing excellence in financial reporting, and that districts receiving the award have demonstrated financial and economic communication at the highest level. The release explains that applicants submit their ACFR for review by financial professionals who provide feedback, that a district's participation can facilitate bond rating and continuing bond-disclosure processes, and that the COE is sponsored by ASBO International Strategic Partner American Fidelity. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is consent-agenda item 5.I, "Establish Fund Depositories and Investment Resolution," prepared for the Troy Board of Education's regular meeting of July 16, 2024. Following the departure of Deputy Superintendent Rick West, the Board must re-adopt the resolution governing where the district's public monies are deposited and invested for the period July through December 2024. The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution, and the resolution is to be incorporated in its entirety into the official minutes.

The resolution recites that public monies belonging to or held for the State, County, or other political units come into the hands of Daniel Trudel, Treasurer of Troy School District, and that Michigan law requires the Board to designate depository banks by resolution. It therefore directs Treasurer Daniel Trudel to deposit and/or invest all public monies, including tax monies, in his name as Treasurer, into the following depository institutions: Bank of America; Citizens Bank; JP Morgan Chase Bank; Comerica Bank; Huntington Bank; Fifth Third Bank; Flagstar Bancorp; MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank); and PNC Bank.

The resolution further provides that district monies may be withdrawn by checks bearing a facsimile signature of Treasurer Daniel Trudel, and in emergencies the handwritten signature of Trudel or of Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, who may sign on the General Fund account and the Payroll account at Bank of America. Monies in the accounts established at PNC Bank for paying Troy Career Center expenses may be withdrawn by checks bearing the handwritten signature of the Troy Career Center Manager, Assistant Manager, or Program Coordinators. The Treasurer is authorized to open or close accounts with the listed institutions when in the district's interest. District funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06, and the Treasurer is authorized to combine money from more than one fund to make an investment authorized by subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Michigan Revised School Code; the maximum amount to be invested is regulated by the school code.

The document closes with a certification block for the Secretary of Troy School District, Oakland County, Michigan, attesting that the resolution was adopted at the meeting held July 16, 2024. Per the meeting minutes, item 5.I was approved as part of the consent agenda by a 6-0 vote (member Haupt absent).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Minutes of a regular meeting of the Troy, Michigan Board of Education held June 20, 2024, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson were present, along with Superintendent Machesky and administrators Montante, Pagel, Fulcher, Smotherman, and West. Approximately 60 members of the public attended.

Public Hearing - 2024/2025 Proposed Budget: Mr. West presented the proposed budget via PowerPoint, addressing tax values, homestead and non-homestead millage, general-fund adjustments and assumptions, ancillary funds, the sinking fund and capital projects fund, student enrollment, the district's foundation-allowance history, and projected revenues and expenditures. The Board noted it had reviewed the proposed budget in its entirety at the June 6 workshop. President Schmidt invited audience questions on the budget; none were asked.

Recognitions: The Board congratulated the Troy United Synchronized Swim Team as 2024 State Champions, with Mr. Fulcher introducing the team and presenting a plaque. Troy High champions named were Rebecca Austin, Erin Choi, Sonia De Donno, Jessica Deng, Ainsley Giorio, Shatakshi Gupta, Ana Sofia Hernandez Gomez, Nidhi Mody, Sei Park, Himasree Puppala, Lucie Rosati, Parker Silagy, Avani Singh, Cate Sivier, Kara Son, Isabel Thommana, Sritha Velireddy, Sasha Vivek, and Sia Wu; Athens champions were Greta Burt, Faith Frederick, Crystal Hensley, McKenzie Johnson, Sakura Mori, and Gwendolyn Schaefer. Coaches Lori Uchwal-Hollier, Erika Mooney, Beth Borland, and Nicole Cervantes were recognized. The Board also recognized the Business Office for again receiving the Association of School Business Officials (ASBO) International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting, honoring the district's Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2023; Deputy Superintendent Rick West, former Finance Director Kandice Moynihan, and the Finance team were credited.

Resolution in Support of Gun Safety and Safe Gun Storage: Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Anne. The resolution's WHEREAS clauses assert that student, teacher, and staff safety is a district priority; that firearm-related death is the leading cause of death among children and adolescents; that firearm death rates for ages 14-17 are 22.5% higher than motor-vehicle death rates; that, per a U.S. Secret Service report, 76% of school-attack perpetrators obtained a firearm from the home of a parent or close relative; that roughly 350 children under 18 unintentionally shoot themselves or someone else each year; that nearly 22,000 Americans die by firearm suicide annually, including over 950 children and teens; and that 47% of firearm owners with children at home do not securely store at least one weapon.

Other agenda items listed include personnel actions - an administrative appointment for Special Education Supervisor (Harker), the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services appointment (Trudel), and ratification of the TEA (Troy Education Association) contract - and Business purchases of serving lines for Boulan, Larson, and Wass elementary schools and UNOX ovens for the IAE, Larson, and Smith Middle School. The extracted text is truncated within the gun-safety resolution, so recorded votes and remaining items are not captured. Minutes were prepared for Secretary Gary N. Hauff (initials GH/jh).

Three items are listed for approval: (A) the minutes of the July 16, 2024 Board of Education meeting; (B) the Treasurer's Report for June 2024; and (C) IA East Schools of Choice, Section 105c 9th Grade for the 2025-2026 school year - a reference to the district's International Academy East participation in Michigan's Section 105c schools-of-choice provision for incoming ninth graders.

As drafted, the document records no vote tally, dollar figures, or additional narrative; it is a procedural instrument enabling the board's approval of the three enumerated consent items.

Directors and supervisors named are Brian Canfield (Director, Employee Services); Rob Carson (Director of Maintenance and Operations); Christine Foren (Supervisor, Special Education); Natalie Haezebrouck (Director of Teaching & Learning); Matt Jansen (Director, Athletics, Continuing Education & Enrichment); Erin Keyser (Director, Early Childhood Program); Kendra Montante (Director, Communications and Strategic Initiatives); Mike Munaco (Supervisor of Career Readiness & Technical Education); Sarah Smotherman (Director, Special Education); Troy Wissink (Director of Technology); and Chantelle Yancy (Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion & Community Relations).

The recommended action is acceptance of the suggested resolution: 'BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Troy Board of Education approve the extension of the contracts of the aforementioned administrators through June 30, 2026, or as otherwise indicated in the administrator's individual contract, without tenure in the administrative positions and subject to the layoff provision in the Administrative Handbook, where applicable and as permitted by law.'
